newsitem.title: INDIA: India, China urged to expand business ties.
newsitem.headline: India, China urged to expand business ties.

text.p: Businessmen and former diplomats, looking ahead to a visit to India this week by China's president, urged India and China on Monday to strengthen cooperation in science, technology, energy and mining.
Participants in a discussion ahead of Chinese President Jiang Zemin's visit to India said the two most populous countries could exploit a range of untapped business opportunities.
Jiang arrives in New Delhi on Thursday and will stay until Sunday. A 50-member business delegation will accompany Jiang, Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and Minister of Foreign Trade Wu Yi.
"The time has come when we need to look at each other more intensely," said C. V. Ranganathan, a former Indian ambassador to China.
India and China face similar problems in the fields of agriculture, energy, environment and health and must interact more closely to find common solutions, Ranganathan said.
Infrastructure bottlenecks in areas like shipping and communications need to be removed in order to give impetus to private sector trade in both countries, he said.
In 1994/95 (April-March) India's exports to China were valued at 8 billion rupees while imports stood at 23.7 billion.
India's exports to China include iron ore, fabrics, drugs and chemicals. Its imports from China include silk, raw coal, machinery and electronic goods.

Shekhar Datta, president of the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), said entrepreneurs in the two countries should form joint ventures and strengthen cooperation in aerospace, electronics, railways, mining and construction.
"China's machinery, power generating equipment, iron and steel smelting equipment, raw silk and some agricultural products could find markets in India," Datta said.
He said India's computer software, iron ore, chrome ore, manganese, pharmaceuticals, leather and medical equipment could find markets in China.
Datta said India could share its expertise in engineering, education and vocational training while China could take advantage of Indian research institutes.

J.N. Dixit, formerly the highest ranking civil servant in the Foreign Ministry, said China considered India important enough to deal with politically and economically. But Jiang's visit to India was part of a South East Asian visit and not focussed only on India, he said.
Jiang will come to India after visiting the Philippines, where he attended the one-day Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum summit, and Nepal, and he will travel on to Pakistan from India.

"In overall terms our endeavour should be to build a working relationship, a practical relationship with China. Our approach should be not to agitate over impractical issues or emotional issues," Dixit said.

New Delhi has recently tried to mend its relations with Beijing by easing off on the decades-old border dispute and reviving trade across the Himalayas suspended since 1959. the two fought a brief border war in 1962.
